[0] everyday_reading (E): Folk meaning: 'for each row and each column' sounds like doing two things side by side or one after the other. In Java the inner loop is a statement in the outer body, so it runs all its passes during each single outer pass (like the hands of a clock).
[1] misconception (M) -> NestedLoopsSequential: wrong rule: The outer loop runs completely, then the inner loop runs completely. Right rule: The inner loop runs all its passes during each single pass of the outer loop.
[2] misconception (M) -> InnerOuterSwapped: wrong rule: The inner loop's variable changes more slowly than the outer loop's. Right rule: The inner loop runs all its passes for each single pass of the outer loop.
[3] misconception (M) -> NestedLoopsLockstep: wrong rule: Nested loops run in step as one loop: both variables change together and both conditions are tested together. Right rule: For each pass of the outer loop the inner loop runs all its passes; the inner variable changes fastest.
[4] misconception (M) -> OuterLoopIgnored: wrong rule: In nested loops only the inner loop repeats; the outer loop runs once. Right rule: The outer loop repeats as its own condition says, and the inner loop runs fully on each outer pass.
[5] misconception (M) -> InnerCounterOverwritesOuter: wrong rule: The inner loop count replaces the outer loop count, so the nested loops run as one loop. Right rule: The two counts multiply: the inner body runs (outer passes) x (inner passes) times.
[6] misconception (M) -> EmptyInnerLoopSkipsRest: wrong rule: If the inner loop runs zero times, the rest of that outer pass is skipped too. Right rule: An inner loop that runs zero times just ends; the statements after it in the outer body still run.
[7] inconsistent_trace (T) -> NestedLoopsSequential: Applies the nested-loop rule (LT) unevenly: resets the inner variable on some outer passes but not others, or advances the outer variable in the middle of the inner loop. (here mixing in: "The outer loop runs completely, then the inner loop runs completely")

[0] names_the_element (N): Nested loops are a loop inside the body of another loop: the outer loop and the inner loop.
[1] states_the_rule (S): Because loops are statements, one can be the body of another; the inner loop iterates all the way through for each iteration of the outer loop.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): Outer init; outer test; [inner init; inner test; inner body; inner update; ... until the inner test fails]; rest of the outer body; outer update; outer test; ... The inner init runs again on every outer pass.
[1] output_prediction (OP): The inner body runs (outer passes) x (inner passes) times: two loops of 1..10 call printf 100 times; DivisorPattern 3 prints 3 rows of 3 entries, each row ending with its row number.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): One outer pass resets the inner variable, runs the complete inner loop, executes the rest of the outer body once, and then updates the outer variable once.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): Usually both loops are for loops: the inner for runs its complete set of passes for every single pass of the outer for.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): Matrix addition uses two nested loops over i and j; matrix multiplication adds a third, innermost loop over k for each dot product.
[2] relation_to_neighbour (R): A plain break ends only the innermost loop; a labeled break is needed when the inner loop must end the outer one too.
[3] relation_to_neighbour (R): Which loop is outside decides the visiting order: row index outside gives row-major order, column index outside gives column-major order.
[4] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Plan: process every pair (i, j) - two-dimensional tables, every row x column of a matrix, every pair of elements; the outer variable is a slow stepper, the inner a fast stepper.

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> NestedLoopsSequential: Swapping the outer and inner loops visits the same pairs in a different order (rows vs columns), which preserves a sum but changes printed layout; moving a statement between the inner body and the outer body changes its count from (outer x inner) to outer.
[1] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Use nested loops when the work ranges over all combinations of two indices (tables, matrices, pairs); expect running time proportional to the product of the pass counts, and prefer a single loop when the second index is a function of the first.
[2] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Without braces, the body of an if, while or for is exactly one statement; indentation does not add statements to it. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: A braceless header followed by two or more indented statements: only the first is controlled, the others run once, after the if/loop, on every input.
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: The inner loop needs its own loop variable. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: Redeclaring the outer variable in the inner header (for (int i ...) { for (int i ...) }): 'variable i is already defined'.
[4] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: The inner loop must update its own variable. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Writing for (int j = 0; j < N; i++) in the inner loop: j never changes, so the inner loop is infinite (or i runs out of range).

A labeled break is needed only when a loop is nested inside another and the inner loop must end the outer one.
